paper_title: Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The idea of AI systems improving their capabilities has long history, from early informal discussions of machines designing more capable successors (Good, 1966) to concrete algorithms for recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Schmidhuber, 1987) and the Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2003). Recent work continues to pursue this goal through modern agentic systems (Fang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2026a). These systems usually improve either the underlying large language model (LLM) or its scaffold, where the latter comprises prompts (Fernando et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024), memory (Xu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026d), tools (Cai et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025), and control logic (Zelikman et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2025) that govern how the model is used. Coding agents provide practical setting for studying self-improvement because they can access and modify their own source code to recursively generate better variants of themselves. Recent systems have improved coding performance by repeatedly modifying this software while keeping the LLM fixed (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Robeyns et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a). Since self-improvement can revisit agents retained in an archive, central design question is not only how to generate self-modifications, but also which modifications should be carried forward during subsequent search. Corresponding author: guodandan@jlu.edu.cn. Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement PREPRINT Figure 1: DGM and HGM exemplify evaluate-and-select strategies, using task-derived evaluation to guide evolution. ELITE instead explores multiple same-parent implementations and integrates compatible mechanisms into descendant, without using downstream task outcomes to guide evolution. Existing approaches answer this question in different ways, but most rely on common principle that we call evaluateand-select to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving. Although their search and selection mechanisms differ, downstream task-derived evidence is used to determine which candidates, groups, or lineages receive subsequent evolutionary effort. DGM uses benchmark performance to guide parent selection from an archive of agents (Zhang et al., 2026b). HGM uses descendant task performance to estimate lineages potential for further improvement (Wang et al., 2026a). GEA uses group-level search and task-based novelty (Weng et al., 2026), while MGM shares information across lineages (Liu et al., 2026). SIFT uses LLM-based comparisons to rank candidate patches (Fu et al., 2026), while RQGM evolves evaluation criteria during search (Iacob et al., 2026). This evaluate-and-select paradigm introduces two limitations. First, obtaining reliable downstream feedback requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on target tasks, making broader exploration increasingly expensive (Xu et al., 2026a; Fu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2026). Second, candidate-level performance scores alone do not specify which implementation mechanisms should be retained or combined. Repeated optimization against fixed evaluation distribution may further encourage benchmark-specific adaptation rather than transferable improvements (Kapoor et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2026). We therefore ask: can coding agents decide which changes to carry forward without downstream candidate task evaluation? key insight is that executable exploration can generate implementation-level evidence for inheritance decisions without downstream candidate task feedback. Implementing focused modifications independently from the same parent makes their mechanisms, interfaces, and dependencies explicit and directly comparable. We can then reason about which mechanisms are complementary, redundant, or conflicting. This allows the next descendant to be constructed from compatible mechanisms without first determining which exploratory child performs best on downstream tasks. Exploratory children thus serve as intermediate implementations that inform integration, with their concrete changes providing the basis for deciding what to inherit. This suggests different route to recursive self-improvement: explore diverse modifications, inspect their implementations, and integrate compatible mechanisms without using downstream task performance to decide what is carried forward. We introduce ELITE, an Explore-then-Integrate approach to self-improvement. ELITE first generates portfolio of focused and diverse improvement hypotheses grounded in concrete limitations of the current agents runtime source. Each hypothesis is implemented independently from the same parent, producing multiple executable alternatives. ELITE then inspects all valid alternatives, identifies mechanisms that are complementary, redundant, conflicting, incomplete, or unnecessarily complex, and integrates compatible mechanisms into one coherent descendant. The integrated descendant is accepted only if deterministic structural and operational checks pass. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide this process. Figure 1 illustrates the difference between ELITE and existing evaluate-and-select approaches. On the 60-task subset of SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for DGM and 88.3% for HGM, while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed evolution time by 8.8 and 3.2, respectively, under our evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, the evolved agent achieves 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Ablations further show that successful task-fitness-free evolution still requires constraints: removing deterministic validity filtering causes performance to collapse. Post-hoc analyses further examine how integration exploits mechanisms across exploratory children and characterize the resulting evolution dynamics. Additional experiments examine an established mini-swe-agent scaffold, direct joint implementation of seven proposals, and evaluation-based child selection in place of mechanism integration. 2 Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement PREPRINT Our contributions are threefold. (1) We observe that coding agents self-modifications are inspectable programs, so which changes to carry forward can be decided from implementation-level evidence rather than downstream task outcomes; we formulate this as the problem of self-improvement without candidate task evaluation. (2) We introduce ELITE, which replaces candidate-level selection with same-parent executable exploration and compatibility-aware mechanism-level integration, while using deterministic checks only for operational validity. (3) We provide empirical evidence that coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation is feasible in our setting, and analyze its evolution dynamics, transfer behavior, and key design components.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Self-improvement in coding agents. Self-improving agents can modify either the underlying model or the agent scaffold, including prompts, memory, tools, workflows, and control logic (Gao et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2026a). Software-engineering agents provide infrastructure for interacting with repositories, development tools, and execution environments (Qian et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025). Automated design methods such as GPTSwarm, ADAS, and AFlow optimize prompts, graph structures, or code-represented workflows (Zhuge et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), while self-referential approaches such as STOP, Gödel Agent, and SICA modify their own scaffolds or implementations (Zelikman et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2025; Robeyns et al., 2025). Coding agents thus provide concrete setting for recursive self-improvement because their executable implementations can be directly modified and used as the basis for subsequent improvements. Research on self-improvement has long history, including self-referential learning and self-modifying policies (Schmidhuber, 1987; Schmidhuber et al., 1997), as well as the Gödel Machines formulation of self-rewriting under provable utility improvement (Schmidhuber, 2003). Within this area, evolutionary search offers one approach to program improvement. Relevant historical foundations include early evolutionary computation (Barricelli et al., 1954; Holland, 1975), genetic programming (Smith, 1980; Cramer, 1985; Dickmanns et al., 1987), and meta-evolution of the improvement procedure itself (Schmidhuber, 1987). Recent LLM-based systems revisit these ideas through executable self-modification. DGM uses benchmark performance to guide archive expansion (Zhang et al., 2026b), while HGM estimates lineage potential from descendant outcomes (Wang et al., 2026a). Hyperagents combines task solving and meta-level improvement in one editable program (Zhang et al., 2026c). GEA and MGM share experience or reuse trajectories and outcomes across groups and lineages (Weng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026); SIFT reduces evaluation cost through LLM-based ranking (Fu et al., 2026), and RQGM co-evolves evaluation criteria (Iacob et al., 2026). Despite their different search and evaluation strategies, these systems retain downstream task-derived evidence to guide evolution. ELITE instead studies whether implementation-level inspection and mechanism integration can construct the next descendant without downstream candidate task evaluation. Implementation-level reasoning for code changes. Recent work in software engineering explores implementationlevel reasoning without executing candidate code. ICE-Score and CodeJudge assess generated code, while RePaCA reasons over buggy and patched implementations to assess patch correctness (Zhuo, 2024; Tong and Zhang, 2024; Fuster-Pena et al., 2026). LLM critics assess repository-level changes, sometimes using reference information such as gold test patches (Yadavally et al., 2025). Agentic Rubrics scores patches against repository-specific criteria (Raghavendra et al., 2026), while SWE-RM learns reward models for fine-grained feedback without unit-test execution (Shum et al., 2026). ASPIRE uses multiple agents to simulate runtime behavior and reason about correctness without code execution (Ramanan et al., 2024). PatchFusion combines edit-level evidence across repair candidates without test outcomes at decision time (Yang et al., 2026). These works address feedback, verification, or patch combination for individual tasks, rather than how an agents own implementation should evolve across generations. ELITE draws on the inspectability of code, using implementation-level reasoning and mechanism integration to construct the next agent without running candidate agents on downstream tasks or using evolved-candidate task outcomes to guide evolution.

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries
sections.content: 3.1 Formalizing Self-Improving Agents Following prior work (Ren et al., 2026a), we formalize an agent configuration as = (θ, Σ), where θ denotes the parameters of the LLM and Σ denotes the agent scaffold, including prompts, memory, tools, and control logic. Selfimprovement proceeds over generations = 0, 1, . . . , 1, with updates abstracted as At+1 = IMPROVE(A0:t; St), where St denotes update-relevant information such as task outcomes, execution trajectories, critiques, verification signals, or modifications (Weng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Each updated agent persists as basis for self-modification. We focus on coding agents with fixed LLM, so At = (θ, Σt) throughout evolution. In our 3 Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement PREPRINT setting, Σt is implemented as source-code repository (Appendix A.2), allowing the scaffold and its modifications to be inspected before downstream evaluation. Such inspection does not establish downstream capability, but can provide implementation-level information (Yadavally et al., 2025; Raghavendra et al., 2026; Shum et al., 2026). 3.2 Evaluate-and-Select Self-improvement Self-improving coding agents organize search differently, but many use downstream task outcomes to guide evolution. We call this pattern evaluate-and-select. Let = {τ1, . . . , τN } be downstream evaluation set, and let R(A, τi) denote the outcome of agent on task τi. Under evaluate-and-select, these outcomes, or estimates obtained from partial evaluation, enter St and influence which agents, groups, or lineages are retained, expanded, or allocated further evaluation. The selection rule may be deterministic or stochastic, may operate over retained historical agents, and may combine task outcomes with lineage statistics, novelty, or resource costs; it need not select single highest-scoring winner. This formulation encompasses range of existing evaluation-driven strategies for selecting or allocating further effort across agents, groups, and lineages (Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a; Weng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Iacob et al., 2026). Obtaining this evidence requires task execution: evaluating candidates on tasks costs rollouts, while adaptive allocation changes the number of evaluations assigned to each candidate but does not eliminate this cost (Fu et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026). Repeated optimization against fixed evaluation distribution may further encourage benchmark-specific adaptation (Kapoor et al., 2024). Separately, agent-level performance scores do not by themselves specify how complementary implementation mechanisms should be combined. These considerations motivate our question: can coding agents decide which changes to carry forward without downstream candidate task evaluation?

sections.title: 4 ELITE: Explore-then-Integrate Self-Improvement
sections.content: Under the formalization in Section 3.1, the two paradigms differ in the information used to update the agent. Evaluateand-select uses downstream task-derived evidence in St to guide which agents or lineages receive further evolutionary effort. ELITE instead uses exploratory implementations and their deterministic validity results; downstream task outcomes of evolved candidates are not used in St to guide integration or next-agent decisions. Rather than selecting an entire child based on estimated performance, ELITE treats implementations as evidence and carries forward compatible mechanisms, shifting the unit of evolutionary decision from whole candidates to implemented mechanisms. At each generation, ELITE follows two stages. Explore generates portfolio of focused improvement hypotheses grounded in limitations of the current agent, each of which is independently implemented from the same parent to produce an executable alternative. Integrate then reasons over the mechanisms realized in these alternatives and reimplements compatible subset into coherent descendant. Deterministic gates are used only to ensure structural and operational validity; no downstream benchmark task, task-solving trajectory, or candidate performance score is used to guide the next-agent decision. 4.1 Limitation-Driven Same-Parent Exploration Limitation-driven hypothesis generation. At generation t, ELITE examines the implementation of the current agent At together with compact evolution history mt, which records prior self-modification instructions and their accompanying code-based rationales. Rather than applying fixed set of mutation categories, proposal operator jointly generates focused improvement hypotheses, Each hypothesis specifies the capability to improve, concrete limitation in the current implementation, focused mechanism for addressing it, and the conditions under which the implementation is complete (Appendix A.3.1). Ht = P(At, mt; K) = {h(1) , . . . , h(K) }. (1) Same-parent executable exploration. Each hypothesis is implemented independently against the same parent At. An implementation operator produces patch (k) , which is applied to At to obtain an executable exploratory child: (k) = E(At, h(k) ), = Apply(At, (k) ), = 1, . . . , K. (2) Because all exploratory children are independently instantiated from the same parent, their modifications provide directly comparable implementation-level alternatives rather than sequentially accumulated changes. This common reference point also makes it possible to reason about mechanisms across children before constructing the next descendant. 4 A(k) Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement PREPRINT Deterministic validity filtering. Before integration, ELITE applies lightweight deterministic gate Gexp(A) {0, 1} to exclude invalid program-level modifications. The gate checks structural and operational validity, such as executability, deployability, required agent interfaces, and permitted modification scope. Python scripts perform compilation, imports, and predefined assertions; Appendix A.5.2 details the checks. The valid alternatives form Vt = A(k) Gexp(A(k) ) = 1 . (3) Importantly, Gexp is an admissibility check rather than measure of downstream capability: it uses no benchmark task outcomes or candidate performance scores. From exploration to integration. Exploration therefore produces set of independently implemented, operationally valid alternatives rather than ranked population. Since no downstream task score identifies winning child in Vt, the remaining decision is not which child should continue as whole, but which mechanisms implemented across these children can be carried forward together. Section 4.2 addresses this decision through compatibility-aware mechanism integration. 4.2 Compatibility-Aware Mechanism Integration From children to mechanisms. Given the valid alternatives Vt, ELITE shifts the decision unit from whole children to their implemented mechanisms. Rather than assigning each child scalar score or predicting which child would perform best, the integrator treats the implementations themselves as evidence. Mechanisms are identified from the intended improvement h(k) together with its realized implementation, allowing mechanism to be considered independently of the child that contains it and jointly with compatible mechanisms realized by other children. For each valid child in Vt, the integrator receives its hypothesis h(k) , and the gate results; the full patch remains available for inspection. The integrator first reviews this evidence across all valid children and then inspects the full implementations of small set of relevant alternatives. The underlying LLM performs integration through implementation-level reasoning guided by the structured prompt in Appendix A.3.3, without separate compatibility model or task-performance predictor. , summary of the realized patch (k) Compatibility-aware mechanism reasoning. Using this implementation-level evidence, the integrator reasons about candidate mechanisms along five dimensions: complementary, when they can operate together; redundant, when they substantially overlap; conflicting, when they make incompatible assumptions about interfaces, state, or control flow; overly complex, when they introduce unnecessary machinery; and incomplete, when the intended mechanism is only partially realized. These judgments determine which mechanisms can be carried forward together, without reducing each child to single predicted-quality score. Based on these judgments, an integration operator constructs an integrated patch against the original parent: int = I(At, Vt), Aint = Apply(At, int ). (4) Importantly, integration operates at the mechanism level rather than by mechanically concatenating or sequentially applying exploratory patches. The selected mechanisms are reimplemented as coherent modification of the common parent At, allowing shared interfaces, dependencies, and control flow to be reconciled when mechanisms interact. Deterministic descendant acceptance. The integrated descendant is accepted only if it passes stricter deterministic gate Gacc(A) {0, 1}, which verifies structural and operational validity. No downstream benchmark task, task-solving trajectory, or candidate performance score is used to determine which mechanisms are integrated or whether the resulting descendant is accepted as the next agent. Downstream evaluation cost. Unlike the direct evaluate-and-select setting in Section 3.2, ELITE requires no downstream candidate-task rollouts for next-agent decisions. Its cost instead comes from generating executable alternatives, inspecting their implementations, and constructing the integrated descendant; this decision cost is independent of the size of downstream evaluation set. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: 5.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate on SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Verified (Deng et al., 2025; Jimenez et al., 2024), and Polyglot (Paul Gauthier, 2024). We use fixed 60-task subset of SWE-bench Pro for the evolution comparison, while SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot serve as transfer benchmarks. After evolution, the resulting agents are frozen and evaluated on the same Pro subset and the two transfer subsets without further adaptation. Detailed benchmark and task-subset information is provided in Appendix A.4. Compared methods and evolution protocol. We compare ELITE with DGM (Zhang et al., 2026b) and HGM (Wang et al., 2026a) using DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.7-Plus. DGM and HGM use outcomes from the Pro subset as evolutionary feedback, whereas ELITE uses no downstream task outcomes during evolution. For each backbone, all methods start from the same scaffold and use the same LLM for both self-modification and task solving, holding the starting agent and model fixed across methods. All three methods have three independent DeepSeek evolution runs; Qwen has three ELITE runs and one run per baseline. full evolution run is the unit of replication. Run-level results and sample SDs are in Appendix A.1.2; configurations are in Appendix A.5. Metrics. We report final task success rate as the primary performance metric. To characterize the resources consumed during self-improvement, we additionally report downstream task-evaluation count, self-modification throughput (Self-Mod./h), estimated evolution-stage token usage, end-to-end wall-clock time, and estimated API cost. 5.2 Main Results Performance. Table 1 summarizes performance across both LLM backbones. Under DeepSeek-V4-Flash, ELITE improves Pro performance from 60.0% to 85.6%, slightly below DGM and HGM at 86.7% and 88.3%, respectively, which use downstream task evaluation feedback to guide evolution. However, its advantage emerges when directly evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot without further evolution, achieving 73.3% and 69.3%, respectively. These results indicate that the improvements produced by ELITE transfer across benchmarks despite the absence of task-specific evaluation feedback during evolution. In contrast, DGM and HGM, evolved on Pro, show limited gains or even regression on these transfer benchmarks. The same pattern holds under Qwen-3.7-Plus, although the trade-off becomes more pronounced: evolving without downstream task feedback is associated with larger performance gap behind DGM and HGM on Pro (45.6% vs. 50.0% and 48.3%), while ELITE still achieves better cross-benchmark transfer (56.7% on Verified and 61.3% on Polyglot). We analyze the evolution process after it has concluded; all downstream task outcomes reported in this analysis are measured post hoc and never exposed to ELITE during evolution. Figure 3(a) compares the seven exploratory children and the integrated descendant from the first accepted step on the same 60 SWE-bench Pro tasks. The exploratory children exhibit substantial outcome variation: six achieve 76.783.3%, while one falls to 3.3%. The integrated descendant reaches 81.7%, outperforming five of the seven children while remaining below the highest exploratory score of 83.3%. This comparison illustrates that ELITE can construct competitive descendant without observing candidate task performance, although integration does not necessarily recover the best-performing exploratory alternative. Figure 3(b) shows the complete = 10 evolution process. The retained agent is updated only when an integrated descendant passes the acceptance gate; otherwise, the current agent is carried forward to the next generation. Across five accepted updates, post-hoc task performance improves overall from 60.0% to 86.7%, despite two intermediate regressions. After the first accepted update reaches 81.7%, subsequent evolution adds further 5.0 percentage points. This non-monotonic trajectory is consistent with the gates intended role: it enforces structural and operational validity without guaranteeing downstream task improvement. An additional sampling-based comparison between integrated descendants and exploratory populations is provided in Appendix A.1.3. Mechanism-level integration. We further inspect the implementations to examine what integration carries forward. Figure 3(c) presents representative composition case in which two same-parent exploratory children independently introduce complementary mechanisms: one enables complete output reading, while the other incorporates exit-status feedback. Rather than selecting either child as the next agent, ELITE integrates both mechanisms into single coherent descendant. In the analyzed DeepSeek run, integration incorporates primary mechanisms from 25 of 41 eligible proposals. Together, the case study and incorporation analysis illustrate how mechanisms from different exploratory children can be carried forward into one descendant without ranking children by downstream task performance. Additional composition and refinement cases are provided in Appendix A.1.4; proposal diversity, gate outcomes, and repository-level analyses are reported in Appendix A.1.1. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced ELITE, an Explore-then-Integrate framework for studying whether coding-agent self-improvement can proceed without downstream candidate task evaluation. Rather than using task outcomes to rank evolved candidates, ELITE explores multiple executable modifications from the same parent and constructs the next agent by reasoning over their implementation mechanisms. Our results provide evidence for the feasibility of substantial coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task feedback in the setting studied here. Limitations. Our evaluation focuses on coding agents and selected benchmark subsets, with limited repetitions for some comparisons. Broader task coverage and additional runs would help characterize variability across settings. ELITE relies on implementation-level reasoning and validity checks to guide evolution; downstream performance can 9 Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement PREPRINT fluctuate across accepted updates, making longer-term evolution an important subject for further study. The current implementation also maintains single lineage. Extending it with an archive of historical agents could preserve alternative evolutionary paths and support broader investigation of search diversity. Appendix A.7 provides further discussion.

The underlying LLM parameters remain fixed, while the scaffold controls tool use, execution feedback, and the problem-solving process. The models programming knowledge and access to source code allow it to identify concrete limitations, such as missing exit-status feedback, blocking output reads, or incomplete parsing. Executable exploration makes the proposed mechanisms, interfaces, and dependencies explicit, providing evidence for integration to reconcile complementary functionality, redundancy, and conflicts. For example, the local code probe in Appendix A.1.4 shows that the integrated implementation combines exit-status feedback with continuous output reading, returning all 100,000 output lines and the correct exit code. Deterministic gates check operational validity, while benchmark evaluations measure the resulting task performance. Evolution dynamics. The observed trajectories show overall gains alongside intermediate variation. In the original DeepSeek run, Pro improves from 81.7% after the first accepted update to 86.7% at the end, with temporary declines following two intermediate accepted updates. In the mini-swe-agent run, ten evolution rounds yield six accepted children. Pro increases from 71.7% initially to 73.3%, 80.0%, and 83.3% for accepted children 1, 3, and 6, respectively  (Table 3)  . These results illustrate improvement over multiple accepted updates. Longer evolution runs would help characterize how progress changes as readily identifiable implementation issues are resolved and remaining bottlenecks depend increasingly on task behavior and interactions among mechanisms. Our evaluation focuses on coding tasks, covering two LLM backbones in the main comparison and an additional scaffoldbackbone combination using mini-swe-agent. The DeepSeek comparison includes three independent runs per method; Qwen baselines and most ablation variants use one run. Evaluation uses selected benchmark subsets. Additional repetitions and broader task coverage would improve the precision of performance estimates and help characterize how improvement depends on the initial scaffold and the underlying models programming capabilities. Beyond coding, evaluation could span diverse task domains, interaction environments, and modalities, including long-horizon tool use (Li et al., 2026b), memory-dependent tasks (He et al., 2026; Nanbo et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026b), web search (Li et al., 2026c; Chen et al., 2026), and multimodal interaction (Li et al., 2026d), while assessing safety and robustness across these settings (Li et al., 2026a; Das et al., 2026). Future work. natural extension is to combine same-parent integration with archive-based search. An archive could retain historical agents, select parent for exploration and integration, and add the resulting valid descendant while preserving alternative lineages. This would allow the search to revisit intermediate stepping stones and explore multiple evolutionary paths. Developing archive-retention and parent-scheduling strategies based on implementation evidence is promising direction for extending ELITE while preserving its independence from downstream candidate task feedback.
